activities.title: From expansion to factorisation
activities.lede: Learn to write a monic quadratic as a product of two linear factors. Work in your exercise book.

notes.body: You should be able to multiply signed integers, list integer factor pairs, collect like terms and expand two brackets. Start by expanding (_x_ + 2)(_x_ + 3) in your book.
(_x_ + _m_)(_x_ + _n_) = _x_^2 + (_m_ + _n_)_x_ + _m_ × _n_. A monic quadratic has leading coefficient 1. To factorise _x_^2 + _b_ × _x_ + _c_, find integers with product c and sum b.

First check for a common factor. For a monic quadratic, test positive divisors of |c| in order and record each distinct magnitude pair once. Apply the signs, compare the sums, verify the selected pair, write the brackets and check by expansion.

If c is positive, the signs agree: both are positive when b is positive, and both are negative when b is negative. If c is negative, the signs differ; the greater absolute value takes the sign of b. If b is zero and c is negative, the two numbers must be opposites.

notes.term: What counts as a complete solution?
notes.body: Record enough working to justify your pair. Keep every sign, then expand to check all three terms. The examples and practice here factorise over the integers. If no integer pair satisfies both conditions, do not force a factorisation.

Both selected numbers are negative, so both brackets contain subtraction.

The product is negative, so the signs differ. The number with greater absolute value takes the sign of the sum.
The remainder rejects 3 as a divisor of 20. Testing 5 would reverse (4, 5), so all distinct magnitude pairs have been found. The greater magnitude must be positive to make the sum positive.

activities.title: Why we split the middle term
activities.lede: Extend the product-and-sum method to quadratics whose leading coefficient is not 1.

notes.body: Write the expression in the form _a_ × _x_^2 + _b_ × _x_ + _c_, with a non-zero a. Remove the greatest common factor first. If the remaining leading coefficient is 1, use the monic method. In the non-monic examples here, the remaining leading coefficient is greater than 1.

Find integers m and n with _m_ × _n_ = _a_ × _c_ and _m_ + _n_ = _b_. Splitting _b_ × _x_ as _m_ × _x_ + _n_ × _x_ preserves the expression. The product condition makes the four terms suitable for factorising by grouping.
Expanding (_p_ × _x_ + _q_)(_r_ × _x_ + _s_) gives _p_ × _r_ × _x_^2 + (_p_ × _s_ + _q_ × _r_)_x_ + _q_ × _s_. The split coefficients ps and qr add to b, and their product is (pr)(qs) = ac.

Group the first two and last two terms. Factor each group so that the bracketed expressions match, then factor out that shared bracket. A negative common factor may be needed. If the brackets do not match, recheck the pair and each sign.
The ac pair splits the middle term; it is not usually the pair of constants in the final brackets. Keep the original leading coefficient and constant, then check your final factors by expansion.

steps.text: Multiply the leading coefficient by the constant to obtain the required product. A positive product and positive sum require two positive numbers.
Test positive divisors in order to find the distinct magnitude pairs. Stop when the next successful divisor reverses a pair already recorded. Then apply the required signs.
Compare the sums in the table with the required sum 7. Each candidate already has the required product.
This pair has product ac and sum b. Use it to split the middle term, not directly as the numbers in the final brackets.
Split 7x as x + 6x. The value of the expression is unchanged.
Factor each pair of terms. Both groups must leave the same bracket.
Factor out the shared bracket (2x + 1). The remaining terms form the other factor.
Expand the factors and collect like terms. The quadratic, linear and constant terms must all match the original expression.

steps.text: Multiply the leading coefficient by the constant to obtain the required product. A positive product and negative sum require two negative numbers.

Split −11x as −2x − 9x.
Take out 2x from the first pair and −3 from the second pair.
steps.note: Taking out +3 would leave −3x + 1 in the second bracket. Take out −3 so both brackets are (3x − 1).

steps.text: Factor out the common bracket (3x − 1).
Expand the factors and collect like terms. The quadratic, linear and constant terms must all match the original expression.
Multiply the leading coefficient by the constant to obtain the required product. The product is negative, so the signs differ. The number with greater absolute value takes the sign of the sum.

Split 5x as 6x − x. Reordering the selected pair is useful for grouping.
Take out 3x from the first pair and −1 from the second pair.
steps.note: The second group is −x − 2. Factoring out −1 changes both signs inside its bracket.
